opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot, because in graph learning scale isn't just about "more rows." When a graph grows, the structure itself changes: degree distributions get more skewed, you get these giant hub nodes, the diameter changes, and neighborhoods can explode in size. So a model that works beautifully on a citation network with a few thousand nodes might behave very differently on a social network or a product graph with billions of edges.

The way we approach it is on a few levels. First, benchmarking. A big reason we put together the Open Graph Benchmark was that the field was evaluating on a handful of tiny datasets, and results there just didn't transfer. So we deliberately built datasets at small, medium, and large scales, across different domains like molecules, knowledge graphs, and citation and product networks, with realistic splits. For example, we split by time or by scaffold rather than randomly, so you're actually testing generalization rather than memorization.

Second, we look at whether the method itself is scalable, not just whether it's accurate. With GraphSAGE, for instance, the whole idea was to move from transductive embeddings, where you learn a vector per node, to an inductive approach where you learn how to aggregate information from a neighborhood. Then you can sample neighborhoods and apply the model to nodes and graphs you never saw during training. When we deployed PinSage at Pinterest, we were working with billions of nodes, and the evaluation there was ultimately very practical: does it train in reasonable time, can you run inference on the whole graph, and does it improve recommendations in offline metrics and then in A/B tests with real users.

And third, we try to be careful about the gap between offline and online, and between small and large. Something we've seen repeatedly is that the ranking of methods can flip as you scale up. Fancy architectures that win on small datasets sometimes overfit or just become computationally infeasible, while simpler, well-engineered models with good sampling and good features win at scale. So we evaluate across that whole range and look at the trend, not one number on one dataset.

More recently, with things like relational deep learning, where you treat an entire relational database as a graph, the question shifts again. Now it's: can one model handle many tables, many entity types, and data that keeps arriving over time? There we focus heavily on temporal evaluation, training on the past and predicting the future, because that's what actually matters when you put these models into production.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can work “beautifully” on a citation network with a few thousand nodes, communicating that predictive methods can perform well on small datasets.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things I think about most, because so much of the work we do in my group at Stanford is about learning from graphs and networks, and the thing about real networks is that they come in wildly different sizes. You might have a small protein interaction network with a few thousand nodes, and then you might have something like the Pinterest graph, which has billions of nodes and tens of billions of edges. And the question is: does the thing you learned actually transfer, or did you just fit the idiosyncrasies of one particular scale?

So the way I think about it, there are really a few different layers to the assessment.

The first one is almost a sanity check, which is: does the method even run? And I don't say that flippantly. A lot of the graph neural network literature early on was evaluated on these tiny citation datasets, Cora, Citeseer, a couple thousand nodes, and methods that look wonderful there completely fall over when you try to apply them to something with hundreds of millions of nodes. That's actually a big part of why we did the PinSage work with Pinterest, and later why we started the Open Graph Benchmark. We wanted datasets at small, medium, and large scale, with realistic splits, so that you're forced to confront the scalability question rather than sweeping it under the rug.

The second layer is about the inductive versus transductive distinction. In a lot of settings you train on one graph and the model only ever sees that graph. But what we really care about is whether the representations generalize to nodes and even entire graphs the model has never seen. That was the core idea behind GraphSAGE: you learn aggregator functions rather than embeddings for specific nodes, and then you can ask, train on a small graph, test on a much larger one, and see how the performance degrades. If it degrades gracefully, that tells you the model has learned something about the local structure that's genuinely scale-independent.

And then the third layer, which I think is the most interesting scientifically, is about what changes qualitatively when scale changes. Because it's not just that big graphs are big. The degree distributions are different, the diameter behaves differently, there are more long-range dependencies, the label distribution often shifts. So we try to be explicit about that. We'll look at performance stratified by node degree, for example, or by distance from the training region, or we'll deliberately subsample the graph at different fractions and look at the learning curve, how does accuracy scale with the amount of data and the size of the structure.

The honest answer is that we don't always get the result we want. Sometimes a model that's great at one scale just isn't the right tool at another, and I think the field has to be comfortable saying that. But that's precisely why having benchmarks that span the range matters so much. If you only ever evaluate at one scale, you really don't know what you have.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish two questions. One is, can the model computationally handle a larger dataset? The other is, does what it learns at one scale still hold at another? Those are very different things.

For graph data, for example, a larger graph may have a different structure, not just more nodes and edges. So I would train at one scale and evaluate across several scales, looking at both predictive performance and computational cost. Does accuracy remain stable? How much memory do we need? How does inference time grow?

And the split matters a lot. If you randomly hold out parts of the same graph, you’re testing something different from predicting on a completely new graph or on data that arrives later. You want the evaluation to reflect the setting where the model will actually be used. That’s what gives you confidence that it generalizes across scales.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating graph models across scales, but does not state that predictive modeling methods perform well on small datasets such as sales-team data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to evaluate at the scale where you actually want to use the model. If a model performs well on a small graph, that doesn’t necessarily mean it will perform well on a graph with millions of nodes. As the graph grows, the connectivity, the amount of information available, and even the distribution of examples can change.

So we look at two things separately: computational scalability—can we train the model and make predictions efficiently?—and predictive performance. We train and test across different graph sizes and different amounts of training data, and examine how performance changes. And we have to be careful about the split: predicting a missing connection among nodes you’ve already seen is a different task from making predictions for entirely new nodes or a new graph. The evaluation needs to reflect the setting we care about.
